title: Cash-flow statements
examples: How do I start the cash flow statement?
What is the difference between profit and cash flow?
Which activities go under operating versus investing?

explain.say: The cash flow statement shows where cash came from and where it went.

draw.text: Cash Flow Statement: Cash In and Out

explain.say: We look at three main sections for cash movements. These are operating, investing, and financing.
For operating activities, we start with net profit and adjust for non-cash items. Depreciation is a common adjustment.
Investing activities track changes in long-term assets. Buying new machinery is a cash outflow here.
Financing activities show transactions with owners or lenders. Receiving a bank loan is a cash inflow.

items: Taking a Bank Loan: Cash Inflow

explain.say: In a real business, if they buy inventory using a trade credit, that is not cash movement. It affects accounts payable instead.

draw.text: Real Life: Credit Purchases are Not Cash

faq.q: Do I always start with net profit?
faq.a: Yes, when using the indirect method, you always begin your operating section with the net profit figure.
asks: Where does the operating section begin?
Must I use net profit as the starting point?

faq.q: What is the difference between profit and cash?
faq.a: Profit includes non-cash items like depreciation. Cash only tracks actual money moving in or out of the business.
asks: Why is profit different from cash?
Are they the same thing for a business?

faq.q: When do I record selling assets?
faq.a: If you sell an asset like machinery, the cash received goes under investing activities. The profit or loss on sale is an adjustment.
asks: Should asset sales go in operating or investing?
How do I account for selling old equipment?

faq.q: Does paying wages count as an investing activity?
faq.a: No, paying wages is part of normal operations. It belongs in the operating activities section.
asks: Where do routine payments like wages go?

faq.q: What is depreciation in this statement?
faq.a: Depreciation is an accounting way of spreading the cost of an asset over time. Since no cash leaves when we record it, we add it back.
asks: Why do I add depreciation back?
What is the purpose of adjusting for depreciation?

facts: The indirect method starts with net profit.
Operating activities relate to day-to-day revenue and expenses.
Investing activities involve changes in long-term assets like Property, Plant, and Equipment.
Financing activities relate to debt and equity transactions.

quiz.say: A company bought a delivery van for cash. This is recorded in:
quiz.why: Buying a long-term asset like a van is always an investing activity.

wrong.0: This is tempting because it is a business expense, but it is an asset purchase, not a routine cost.
wrong.1: This is tempting because it involves a large sum, but financing deals are only with owners or banks.
wrong.2: This is incorrect because the purchase clearly fits one of the three defined sections.

quiz.say: If a business receives cash from selling old office furniture, it goes under:
quiz.why: Selling fixed assets, even small ones, falls under the category of investing activities.

wrong.0: Financing deals concern money from lenders or owners, not asset sales.
wrong.1: The statement must place the transaction in only one primary section.
wrong.3: While it relates to the business, the sale of fixed assets is specifically classified as investing.

quiz.why: Since depreciation is a non-cash expense, we add it back to net profit to find the true cash flow.

wrong.0: Ignoring it means we fail to adjust for the non-cash nature of the expense.
wrong.1: There is no mathematical reason to multiply this adjustment by two.
wrong.3: Subtracting it would mean we are treating it like a cash outflow, which it is not.
